openings.name: The Epistolary or "Found Document" Hook
openings.text:
Start the chapter outside the immediate narrative using an artifact. Excellent for world-building without info-dumping.
 Examples: A snippet from a military tribunal transcript, an excerpt from an in-universe historical text, a captain’s log, a diagnostic report on a failing piece of machinery, or a fragmented radio transmission from an Okinawa quarantine zone.

openings.name: The In Media Res Action Drop
openings.text:
Drop the reader directly into the middle of an action sequence with no preamble or context. Let them catch up as the scene unfolds.
 Execution: Begin mid-swing, mid-shout, or mid-retreat. Avoid explaining why the characters are running until paragraph three or four.

openings.name: The Micro-Sensory Focus
openings.text:
Instead of describing the whole room or setting, start with extreme hyper-focus on a single, often uncomfortable, sensory detail. 
 Execution: The smell of ozone, the rhythmic dripping of condensation on a metal grate, the grit of sand between teeth, or the specific pitch of a distant siren.

openings.name: The Cinematic "Wide-to-Narrow" Pan
openings.text:
Establish the macro scale of the setting before zooming in on the micro reality of your point-of-view character.
 Execution: Describe the massive scale of a fleet in orbit, the sprawling geography of an island containment zone, or the architecture of a facility, then narrow the lens sharply down to the protagonist lacing up their boots in a cramped room.

openings.name: The Thematic Thesis (The "Victor Hugo" Opening)
openings.text:
Open with a broad philosophical statement, an observation about human nature, or a reflection on the mechanics of the universe.
 Execution: State a universal "truth" about war, justice, or fear, and then immediately juxtapose it with the specific, messy reality your character is currently facing.

openings.name: The Disembodied Dialogue
openings.text:
Start with a line of dialogue—or an exchange of dialogue—before the reader knows who is speaking or where they are.
 Execution: Use a sharp, provocative, or confusing statement. "Cut the hardline," or "She’s not breathing." Follow the exchange for a few beats before grounding the reader in the setting.

openings.name: The Temporal Marker or "Ticking Clock"
openings.text:
Orient the reader purely through time, establishing immediate dread or urgency.
 Execution: "It had been forty-two hours since the last transmission," or "Sunrise was exactly three minutes away."

openings.name: The Subverted Routine
openings.text:
Begin by describing a character going through a mundane, highly practiced routine, and end the opening paragraph by breaking that routine entirely.
 Execution: The familiar process of breaking down a rifle, preparing legal briefs, or running a perimeter check, violently interrupted by the inciting incident of the chapter.

openings.name: The Ominous Fact / Dramatic Irony
openings.text:
State a cold, hard fact that the reader knows, the narrator knows, but the characters in the scene do not know.
 Execution: "No one in the squad knew that the floor beneath them was rigged to blow."

openings.name: The Memory or Dream Transition
openings.text:
Open with a surreal or fragmented memory that seamlessly—or jarringly—bleeds into the present reality.
 Execution: A memory of a peaceful moment or a past trauma that is interrupted by a character being shaken awake or snapping back to attention in a hostile environment.

openings.name: The Objective Status Report
openings.text:
Strip away all emotion and describe the state of the protagonist or the squad with cold, clinical detachment.
 Execution: List the remaining ammunition, the physical injuries, the temperature drops, or the structural integrity of their shelter as an itemized inventory of desperation.

openings.name: The Flash-Forward Setup
openings.text: Open with the chaotic climax of the chapter, then immediately hit the reader with "Four hours earlier," forcing them to read just to figure out how things went so wrong.

openings.name: The Retrospective Regret
openings.text: The narrator speaks from a point in the future, framing the upcoming scene with dread. (Example: "If she had known that was the last time she’d see the sun, she wouldn't have spent it compiling code.")

openings.name: The "Negative Space" Opening
openings.text: Describe exactly what is missing from a scene to establish the tone. (Example: "There was no static on the comms, no ambient hum from the servers, and worse, no screaming.")

openings.name: The "How We Got Here" Rapid Recap
openings.text: A cynical or breathless one-paragraph summary of the disastrous decisions that led to the current moment.

openings.name: The Lingering Hangover
openings.text:
Start entirely focused on the physical or emotional wreckage left by the previous chapter before moving the plot forward.
---

openings.name: The Immediate Dilemma
openings.text: Open with a harsh, binary choice the protagonist is actively weighing. (Example: "Cut the oxygen to the lower decks, or let the cereus parasite reach the bridge.")

openings.name: The Deceptive Calm
openings.text: Paint a picture of perfect, pristine safety that is so idyllic the reader immediately knows something terrible is about to happen.

openings.name: The Obsessive Tic
openings.text: Focus entirely on a character’s physical coping mechanism—picking at a thumbnail, disassembling and reassembling a mag, tapping a rhythm on a console—to show, not tell, their anxiety.

openings.name: The Unanswered Question
openings.text: Start the chapter with an internal or spoken question that frames the entire thematic conflict of the scene.

openings.name: The List
openings.text: A rapid-fire, stream-of-consciousness catalog of a character's racing thoughts, priorities, or physical injuries.

openings.name: The Shift in Perspective
openings.text:
Open the chapter from the point of view of an NPC, an enemy combatant, or even the hostile environment itself watching the protagonist approach.
---

openings.name: The Biological Extreme Close-Up
openings.text: Bypass the surroundings entirely and start with visceral, uncomfortable bodily realities. (Example: "Lactic acid burned like battery fluid in his calves, and his pulse hammered a desperate warning against his eardrums.")

openings.name: The Weather/Atmosphere Override
openings.text: Make the environment the primary antagonist of the first paragraph. Acid rain, suffocating humidity, or a vacuum drop that demands immediate attention.

openings.name: The Auditory Assault
openings.text: Describe a sudden, deafening noise—or a highly specific, terrifying sound—that shatters a quiet moment.

openings.name: The Topographical Orientation
openings.text:
Orient the reader strictly by geography and geometry, emphasizing isolation or tactical disadvantage. (Example: "They were four hundred meters below sea level, backed against a limestone ridge.")
---

openings.name: The Bureaucratic Preamble
openings.text: Open with the dry, impenetrable text of a legal statute, corporate policy, or treaty that the characters are about to violently violate, setting the stage for a tense courtroom or tribunal.

openings.name: The Lore/Mythology Drop
openings.text: Briefly recount an ancient myth, historical battle, or local legend that perfectly mirrors the current predicament.

openings.name: The Paradox
openings.text: Start with a deliberately contradictory statement that forces the reader to pause and recalibrate. (Example: "The only thing more dangerous than a loaded weapon was an empty courtroom.")

openings.name: The Institutional Critique
openings.text: The narrator offers a cynical observation about the military, the legal system, or the government that grounds the scene in systemic frustration.

openings.name: The Technical Diagnostic
openings.text:
Open with pure, unadulterated jargon or a system output that implies disaster to anyone who knows how to read it. (Example: "Core temp: 180°C. Containment field: 10%. Override protocol: offline.")
6. Classical & Epic (Greco-Roman)

openings.name: The Invocation of the Muse
openings.text:
Open by formally asking a god, muse, or higher power to grant the telling — which doubles as a thesis statement of the work's subject.


Touchstone: The Iliad begins by calling on the goddess to sing the wrath of Achilles; the Aeneid announces "arms and the man."
Spin: Open a chapter as a declassified preamble that "invokes" its authorizing body — a request to the archive, the tribunal, or the AI itself to render what follows.

openings.name: The Programmatic Proem
openings.text:
The narrator states up front what this account is, why it matters, and how it was gathered — establishing authority before any events.


Touchstone: Herodotus opens by presenting his inquiry; Thucydides opens by arguing his war is the greatest yet recorded.
Spin: A field historian or after-action analyst frames the chapter by claiming its significance before showing it.

openings.name: The Epic Catalogue (kin to your #21, The List)
openings.text:
Open with a sweeping enumeration — forces, ships, names, holdings — where the sheer scale is the effect.


Touchstone: Homer's Catalogue of Ships.
Spin: A muster roll, a manifest, or a casualty ledger read as grim poetry.



7. Sacred & Scriptural Openings

openings.name: The Cosmogonic "In the Beginning"
openings.text:
Start at an origin point — of a world, an order, a conflict — in a register of creation.


Touchstone: Genesis and the Gospel of John both open at the literal beginning of things.
Spin: The origin of the parasite, the facility, or the war, narrated as a creation myth the in-universe culture now repeats.

openings.name: The Naming of the Power (Invocation / Basmala)
openings.text:
Begin by naming the authority under whose sign the text proceeds.


Touchstone: Many Arabic and Persian works open by naming God; Ferdowsi's Shahnameh opens in the name of the Lord of soul and wisdom.
Spin: A chapter that opens under the seal and authority of an agency — "By order of…" — before a word of narrative.

openings.name: The Prophetic Call / Vision Commission
openings.text:
Open with a figure being summoned — given a vision, a word, or a burden they did not ask for.


Touchstone: The prophetic books open with the word coming to someone.
Spin: A soldier or analyst receiving an order, a transmission, or a hallucination that conscripts them into the chapter's events.

openings.name: The Parable Frame
openings.text:
Begin obliquely with a small illustrative story whose meaning the chapter will detonate.


Touchstone: "A certain man went down…" — the parable's deliberately generic opening.
Spin: A barracks legend or a piece of in-universe folklore told straight, then weaponized by events.



8. Frame-Tale & Oral-Transmission Markers (cross-cultural)

openings.name: The Frame Return
openings.text:
Don't open on the action — open on the outer story resuming, the teller picking the thread back up.


Touchstone: The Thousand and One Nights returns each night to Scheherazade; the Canterbury Tales and Decameron return to their travelers.
Spin: Return to the interrogation room, the debrief, or Booker-style narrator between embedded accounts.

openings.name: The Transmission Tag
openings.text:
Open with the oral marker that flags this as received knowledge, passed hand to hand.


Touchstone: Chinese vernacular novels open with huàshuō ("the story goes that…"); countless traditions open "It is related that…" / "They say…".
Spin: "The record states…" / "Per the recovered log…" — your found-document aesthetic as a recurring incantation.

openings.name: The Chapter-Argument Couplet
openings.text:
Open every chapter with a short verse or paired-line summary of what it contains — a built-in headline.


Touchstone: The Chinese zhanghui novel (e.g., Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Water Margin) heads each hui with a balanced couplet.
Spin: A two-line classified subject-header per chapter, redaction-bar included — a DOMARE table of contents that's also poetry.

openings.name: The Call to Attention
openings.text:
Open by demanding the audience listen — a verbal seizing of the room.


Touchstone: Beowulf opens with "Hwæt!"; medieval minstrels opened with "Oyez"; West African griots open by asking leave to tell.
Spin: A broadcast cold-open — "All stations, all stations" — or an instructor silencing a briefing room.



9. East Asian Traditions

openings.name: The "Long Ago Now" Tale-Opener
openings.text:
A fixed formula that drops the listener into mythic past-time instantly.


Touchstone: Japanese setsuwa open Ima wa mukashi ("now it is long ago"); folktales open mukashi mukashi.
Spin: "Before the quarantine, there was a city…" — a fairy-tale cadence applied to recent, traumatic history.

openings.name: The Seasonal Threshold
openings.text:
Open not on plot but on the season — a single seasonal image that sets the entire emotional weather.


Touchstone: The Pillow Book opens "In spring, the dawn"; the renga/haiku tradition anchors openings to a season-word (kigo).
Spin: Open on Okinawa's humidity, typhoon pressure, or the specific light of a season before any character speaks.

openings.name: The Impermanence Bell (mono no aware)
openings.text:
Open on transience itself — a sound or image that announces that all of this is already passing.


Touchstone: The Tale of the Heike opens on the Gion temple bell echoing the impermanence of all things.
Spin: The cooling tick of a dead reactor, a last functioning beacon — sound as a memento mori for the chapter.

openings.name: The Following-the-Brush Drift (zuihitsu)
openings.text:
Open in apparent idleness, one associative thought leading to the next, until the drift lands somewhere sharp.


Touchstone: Kenkō's Tsurezuregusa opens "in idleness"; Sei Shōnagon's lists wander by association.
Spin: A journaling voice (your Prima Materia register) meandering through small observations before the chapter's blade drops.

openings.name: The Oblique Court Introduction
openings.text:
Introduce a central figure indirectly — by rank, rumor, or circumstance — without naming them.


Touchstone: The Tale of Genji opens "in a certain reign there was a lady…".
Spin: "There was an officer whose name the files no longer carry…" — introduction by redaction.

openings.name: The Cosmological-Historical Frame
openings.text:
Open with a vast cyclical law of history, then drop into the human-scale instance of it.


Touchstone: Three Kingdoms opens on the maxim that the empire long divided must unite, long united must divide.
Spin: A line on the eternal cycle of containment and breach, then one soldier at one airlock.

openings.name: The Kishōtenketsu Pivot
openings.text:
Structure the opening around a coming turn rather than a conflict — introduction, development, then an oblique twist that recontextualizes, then reconciliation. Tension comes from juxtaposition, not collision.


Touchstone: The four-act ki-shō-ten-ketsu logic underlying much East Asian narrative.
Spin: Open two unrelated threads calmly; let the "ten" be the reader's realization that they're the same event seen twice.



10. Persian, Arabic & Islamicate

openings.name: The Praise-Prelude
openings.text:
Open with a passage of praise or reflection before the narrative proper — a tuning of the instrument.


Touchstone: Persian masnavi (Rumi, Ferdowsi) traditionally open with praise of the divine and of intellect.
Spin: An epigraph venerating the institution, the mission, or the machine — sincere on its face, ironic in context.

openings.name: The Object That Speaks Its Grief
openings.text:
Open in the voice of a thing, whose lament becomes the chapter's theme.


Touchstone: Rumi's Masnavi opens with the reed-flute lamenting its separation from the reed bed.
Spin: A salvaged black box, a dying AI, or a weapon "narrating" its own use and longing.

openings.name: "Once There Was, Once There Was Not"
openings.text:
Open with a paradox that suspends the tale between truth and fiction.


Touchstone: The Persian folk-opener yeki bud yeki nabud.
Spin: "It happened, and the record denies it happened" — perfect for a story about classification and deniability.

openings.name: The Maqāma Encounter
openings.text:
Open with a wandering narrator stumbling onto an eloquent stranger/trickster whose performance is the chapter.


Touchstone: The Arabic maqāmāt of al-Harīrī — rhymed prose, recurring rogue.
Spin: A recurring informant or con artist the protagonist keeps re-encountering in new disguises.



11. South Asian

openings.name: The Benediction Verse (maṅgalācaraṇa)
openings.text:
Open with a short auspicious invocation that blesses the undertaking of the text.


Touchstone: The conventional invocatory verse opening classical Sanskrit works.
Spin: A one-line "may this record survive its readers" charm heading the chapter.

openings.name: The Nested Didactic Tale
openings.text:
Open a story inside a story inside a lesson — frames within frames, each teaching.


Touchstone: The Panchatantra / Hitopadesha embed fables several layers deep.
Spin: A mentor tells a cadet a story; inside it, a character tells another story that's the real warning.

openings.name: The Mythic-Time Placement
openings.text:
Locate the chapter in a fixed legendary past with a formulaic stamp.


Touchstone: Jātaka tales open "long ago, when Brahmadatta reigned in Benares…".
Spin: "In the years the Affairs Office still answered its phones…" — a stamp that dates the chapter to a lost era.



12. Oral Epic & Indigenous Traditions

openings.name: The Teller's Self-Authentication
openings.text:
The narrator opens by naming themselves and their right to tell this — the credential is the opening.


Touchstone: In the Sundiata epic, the griot (jeli) opens by declaring who he is and that he is the keeper of the word.
Spin: A narrator who opens by establishing their clearance and chain of custody for the account.

openings.name: The Saga Deadpan
openings.text:
Open with flat, unadorned fact: a man, where he lived, who his father was. No drama — the drama comes later, and the flatness makes it land harder.


Touchstone: Icelandic family sagas (Njáls saga, Egils saga) open with terse genealogy and geography.
Spin: "There was a sergeant named ——. He was posted to the ridge. His mother had served before him." Cold, then catastrophic.

openings.name: The Singer's Desire
openings.text:
Open by stating the urge to tell — the telling framed as something welling up and demanding release.


Touchstone: The Finnish Kalevala opens with the singer declaring a mind/desire to sing.
Spin: A character compelled to record testimony they were ordered to forget.

openings.name: Seasonal / Ceremonial Gating
openings.text:
The opening signals that a story may only be told under certain conditions — and the telling itself is therefore a transgression or a rite.


Touchstone: In several Indigenous North American traditions, including Diné (Navajo) practice, certain stories are properly told only in winter; the time of telling is part of the story's meaning. (Worth handling with care and research rather than imitation — but the underlying device, "this may only be spoken now, and that's why it matters," is powerful.)
Spin: A log that "may only be opened after the operation is dead" — the reader breaking a seal by reading.

openings.name: Mythic-Time Entry
openings.text:
Open in an undifferentiated originary time before the present order.


Touchstone: Australian Aboriginal storytelling opens in the Dreaming; many traditions open "when the animals were still people."
Spin: Before the cordon, before the maps were reclassified — a chapter that opens in the world's prior shape.



13. Medieval & Renaissance European

openings.name: The Dream-Vision Threshold
openings.text:
The narrator falls asleep (or into reverie) and the chapter unfolds as an allegorical dream.


Touchstone: Dante opens the Commedia midway through life's journey, lost; Piers Plowman and Pearl open into dreams.
Spin: A drugged, concussed, or cryo-thawed POV whose chapter blurs vision and reality — and you decide later which it was.

openings.name: The Dedicatory Epistle
openings.text:
Open with an address to a patron or reader about the work, before the work begins.


Touchstone: Renaissance works routinely open with a letter to a patron.
Spin: A transmittal memo ("Per your request, find enclosed…") heading a chapter of recovered material.

openings.name: The Estates Catalogue
openings.text:
Open by parading a gallery of character-types one after another, sketching a whole social world.


Touchstone: The General Prologue of the Canterbury Tales introduces its pilgrims in turn.
Spin: A roll-call of a squad or a station's personnel, each thumbnail loaded with foreshadowing.

openings.name: The Pseudo-Translation Frame (kin to your #1, Found Document)
openings.text:
Open by insisting the text is merely a translation or transcription of a real document the author found.


Touchstone: Don Quixote attributes itself to a found Arabic manuscript; The Castle of Otranto posed as a translated medieval chronicle.
Spin: "Translated from the recovered field journal; bracketed text reconstructed." The conceit you already love, with the translator's own voice intruding.



14. The Novel, 18th–19th Century

openings.name: The Aphoristic Social Truth (kin to your #5, Thematic Thesis)
openings.text:
Open with a confident universal maxim — which the chapter then proceeds to complicate or demolish.


Touchstone: Austen opens Pride and Prejudice on a "truth universally acknowledged"; Tolstoy opens Anna Karenina on happy versus unhappy families.
Spin: "Every containment failure is alike; every cover-up fails in its own way."

openings.name: The Essayistic Preamble
openings.text:
Open the chapter with the narrator's standalone essay or digression, only loosely tethered to the plot.


Touchstone: Fielding opens each book of Tom Jones with a discursive chapter.
Spin: A short treatise on bureaucracy, fear, or signal latency before the chapter's action — your Institutional Critique (#30) at full length.

openings.name: The Direct Self-Naming / Address
openings.text:
Open by speaking straight to the reader, often by naming the narrator.


Touchstone: Moby-Dick opens by inviting the reader to call him Ishmael.
Spin: A testimony that opens "You can call me whatever the file calls me" — identity as something assigned, not owned.

openings.name: The Panoramic Omniscient Establishing Shot (kin to your #4, Wide-to-Narrow)
openings.text:
Open with a god's-eye sweep over a whole city or era before descending — but held longer, more essayistic, more atmospheric.


Touchstone: Bleak House opens on London fog; A Tale of Two Cities on the age of extremes.
Spin: A long aerial pass over the quarantined island as a living organism before you find your one soldier in it.

openings.name: The Autobiographical Birth
openings.text:
Open a life-story at its literal start, with the narrator framing whether they'll even prove to be the hero.


Touchstone: David Copperfield opens by questioning whether the narrator is the hero of his own life.
Spin: A character's after-action statement that opens by doubting they were ever the protagonist of the operation.



15. Modernist & Contemporary

openings.name: The Mid-Thought Consciousness
openings.text:
Drop into the unpunctuated flow of a mind already in motion — no scene-setting, just interiority.


Touchstone: Woolf opens Mrs Dalloway mid-errand, in Clarissa's thought.
Spin: Open inside a pilot's task-saturated headspace, the prose itself fragmenting under G-load.

openings.name: The Confessional Frame
openings.text:
Open with an admission that colors everything after — the narrator confessing the difficulty or shame of telling.


Touchstone: Ford Madox Ford opens The Good Soldier by calling it the saddest story he's heard.
Spin: A debrief that opens "I've told this wrong every time I've told it" — an unreliable-witness flag raised on line one.

openings.name: The Second-Person Address
openings.text:
Make the reader the protagonist; "you" do the chapter's actions.


Touchstone: Calvino's If on a winter's night a traveler addresses the reader as the one acting.
Spin: A training-simulation or interrogation chapter narrated as "You enter the room. You are not supposed to be here."

openings.name: The Retrospective-Prospective Fold
openings.text:
Open from a future vantage looking back, compressing decades into one sentence that pivots from doom to a tender memory.


Touchstone: García Márquez opens One Hundred Years of Solitude with a man before a firing squad recalling the distant day he first saw ice. (Paraphrased — the line is in copyright.)
Spin: "Years after the tribunal, what she'd remember was not the verdict but the smell of the courtroom's air conditioning." Fuses your #12 (Flash-Forward) and #13 (Retrospective Regret) into one motion.

openings.name: The Matter-of-Fact Marvelous
openings.text:
State the impossible in the flat register of the ordinary — no astonishment, which makes it more unsettling.


Touchstone: Magical realism's signature deadpan toward the supernatural.
Spin: "The parasite had been speaking for three days. Nobody on the night shift found this remarkable anymore."

openings.name: The Metafictional Aside
openings.text:
Open by acknowledging the artifact — that this is a record, a book, a constructed account — and letting that destabilize the reader.


Touchstone: The self-aware narrator who reminds you you're reading.
Spin: A chapter that opens by noting which pages of itself are missing, or that it was assembled by an AI from partial logs (Booker's voice).



16. Genre Signatures

openings.name: The Recurring Invented Epigraph (systematized #1)
openings.text:
Head every chapter with a quotation from a fictional in-world source, building a second, ghostly text alongside the novel.


Touchstone: Dune heads chapters with the writings of Princess Irulan; Foundation uses Encyclopedia Galactica entries.
Spin: Each chapter opens with a DOMARE memo, a redacted field manual line, or a Booker annotation — your aesthetic's natural home.

openings.name: The Noir Weather-and-Mood
openings.text:
Open on weather and atmosphere doing the emotional work, voice dripping with weary attitude.


Touchstone: The hardboiled detective opening — climate as character, cynicism as register.
Spin: Okinawan rain on a tin roof, a narrator too tired to be afraid yet.

openings.name: The Western Landscape-as-Fate
openings.text:
Open on a vast, indifferent landscape that dwarfs and predetermines the human figures crossing it.


Touchstone: The frontier opening where the land is the real antagonist.
Spin: A salt flat, a containment perimeter, an ocean trench — geography as verdict. (Overlaps your #26, Topographical Orientation, but at mythic scale.)

openings.name: The Procedural Slug-Line
openings.text:
Open with a formatted operational header — time, grid, unit, status — that reads as authentic documentation.


Touchstone: The military/thriller timestamp opening ("0347 LOCAL — SECTOR 7 — EYES ONLY").
Spin: Your native dialect. Fuse with #31 (Technical Diagnostic) for a header that's already a disaster to the trained reader.

openings.name: The Newsreel / Documentary Montage
openings.text:
Open with a collage of headlines, broadcast fragments, ad copy, and overheard speech — the era's noise before the individual story.


Touchstone: Dos Passos's newsreel sections in U.S.A.
Spin: A scroll of intercepted comms, propaganda banners, and panic-channel chatter before you cut to one quiet character inside the noise.

structures.name: Kishōtenketsu
structures.text: [Japanese/Chinese verse] — four movements resolved by a context-shifting twist, not conflict.

structures.name: Sonata-Allegro
structures.text: [Classical music] — two opposed themes stated, fractured in development, the antagonist-theme resolved "home."

structures.name: The Five Sandhis
structures.text: [Sanskrit drama] — five junctures with a mandatory hesitation/doubt beat (vimarśa) before resolution.

structures.name: Aristotelian Microcosm
structures.text: [Greek] — the chapter as a complete miniature story ending at equilibrium.

structures.name: Scene–Sequel
structures.text: [Swain] — Goal/Conflict/Disaster, then Reaction/Dilemma/Decision.

structures.name: MICE Quotient
structures.text: [Card] — resolve one thread-type (Milieu/Idea/Character/Event) before opening the next.

structures.name: In Media Res Sandwich
structures.text: — open at the crisis, drop back for minimal context, blast past the opening.

structures.name: Jo-ha-kyū
structures.text: [Japanese; Hindustani raga variant] — slow → break → rapid accelerando; the raga variant binds the whole to one emotion and one hour.

structures.name: Shōnen Escalation
structures.text: [manga] — power gap → analysis → beating → discover the hidden rule → reversal.

structures.name: Mecha Launch Sequence
structures.text: [anime] — ritual synchronized buildup → massive kinetic release.

structures.name: Ticking Clock / Real-Time
structures.text: — chapter maps 1:1 to clock time; fragmented sentences burn the minutes.

structures.name: Cathartic Release
structures.text: — inverted tension: open at maximum, structure is one long exhale to safety.

structures.name: Theme & Variations
structures.text: [music] — one scene-template replayed, each pass transformed.

structures.name: Rondo (ABACA)
structures.text: [music] — a refrain-scene returns between contrasting episodes, accruing menace.

structures.name: Colotomic Cycle
structures.text: [Javanese gamelan] — stratified loops of different lengths all coinciding on a recurring "gong."

structures.name: Sestina
structures.text: [Occitan troubadour] — six motifs recur every scene in a fixed rotating permutation.

structures.name: Incremental Repetition
structures.text: [folk ballad] — near-identical beats, one variable advanced toward doom.

structures.name: The Snowball Circle
structures.text: [Inuit-attributed — verify provenance] — circular accretion; ends where it began, fundamentally altered.

structures.name: Ring Composition / Chiasmus
structures.text: [ancient, near-universal] — ABCBA fold; the center carries the meaning, the second half inverts the first.

structures.name: Crab Canon / Retrograde
structures.text: [Bach] — the second half is the first half exactly reversed.

structures.name: Pantoum
structures.text: [Malay] — each scene reuses the prior's back half; closes on its own opening line. Kin: 19, 20.

structures.name: Mugen Noh
structures.text: [Japanese dream-theatre] — a stranger revealed as a revenant; part two re-enacts the buried trauma for release.

structures.name: Rashomon Convergence
structures.text: [Akutagawa/Kurosawa] — one event restaged 3–4× from conflicting POVs; truth in the negative space.

structures.name: Whodunnit Reverse-Engineer
structures.text: — open on the solution; dissect backward through the logic that produced it.

structures.name: Fugue State / Dream Logic
structures.text: — transitions by sensory association, not chronology or geography.

structures.name: Russian Matryoshka
structures.text: — story-within-story-within-memory, then pulled all the way back out.

structures.name: Renga Link-and-Shift
structures.text: [Japanese linked verse] — each scene links only to its neighbor and is forbidden to look back.

structures.name: Flâneur Drift
structures.text: [French] — a goalless wandering observer accretes atmosphere until a realization lands.

structures.name: Braided POV / Double Helix
structures.text: — two threads alternate in bursts that shorten until they violently intersect.

structures.name: The True Fugue
structures.text: [Baroque counterpoint] — a subject imitated by successive voices, overlapping to a stretto collision. Distinct from 25.

structures.name: Bunraku Channel-Split
structures.text: [Japanese puppet theatre] — description, all dialogue, and emotional "scoring" run as three parallel channels.

structures.name: Greek Chorus
structures.text: — main action periodically interrupted by a collective commenting voice.

structures.name: Exquisite Corpse
structures.text: [Surrealist] — sections composed blind to each other; the surreal joins are the point.

structures.name: French Dialectic
structures.text: [Plan Dialectique] — thesis / antithesis / synthesis.

structures.name: Scholastic Quaestio
structures.text: [medieval — Aquinas] — objections stacked / sed contra / I answer / point-by-point replies. Sharper kin of 34.

structures.name: The Sugya
structures.text: [Talmudic] — question, objection, resolution; the rejected minority opinion is preserved on the page.

structures.name: Classical Oration
structures.text: [Cicero/Quintilian] — exordium, narratio, partitio, confirmatio, refutatio, peroratio.

structures.name: Eight-Legged Essay / Bagu
structures.text: [Chinese] — perfectly symmetrical balanced-pair argument.

structures.name: Chreia Elaboration
structures.text: [ancient rhetoric] — one maxim expanded through eight fixed moves.

structures.name: Cross-Examination Spiral
structures.text: — broad questions circling inward, accelerating, to a fatal contradiction.

structures.name: Burden of Proof
structures.text: — begin from assumed guilt; systematically dismantle it.

structures.name: Objection Volley
structures.text: — staccato: every rhythm violently interrupted by a counter.

structures.name: Deposition Breakdown
structures.text: — clinical Q&A transcript alternating with the messy remembered reality.

structures.name: Evidence Chain
structures.text: — POV follows one artifact hand to hand; stakes ride on who holds it.

structures.name: Recursive Loop / Iteration
structures.text: [computational] — repeat the scenario, accumulate knowledge, until the loop breaks.

structures.name: Version Control / Git Pacing
structures.text: — the text visibly overwrites itself; drafts replace drafts in real time.

structures.name: Boolean Trap (If/Then)
structures.text: — progress only when binary conditions are met; failure is a dead end.

structures.name: Stack Trace
structures.text: — begin at the crash; retrace the exact cascade back to the origin fault.

structures.name: Memory Leak
structures.text: — the narration degrades, fragmenting until only raw emotion remains.

structures.name: Epistolary Mosaic
structures.text: — in-world documents arranged so the reader connects the dots. Kin: 51.

structures.name: The Cento
structures.text: [late-antique] — built entirely from borrowed/quoted fragments repurposed into new meaning. Kin: 50.

structures.name: The Cut-Up
structures.text: [Dada → Burroughs] — two source texts sliced and interleaved for forced collision. Kin: 53.

structures.name: Kuleshov Effect
structures.text: [Soviet montage] — unrelated scenes juxtaposed without transition; the reader infers the link. Kin: 52.

structures.name: Kamishibai Tableau
structures.text: [Japanese paper theatre] — freeze into discrete, intensely detailed snapshots. Inverse of 72.

structures.name: Brechtian Verfremdungseffekt
structures.text: [German] — deliberately break immersion with sterile facts to force objectivity.

structures.name: The Tristram Shandy Engine
structures.text: [Sterne] — progress by non-progress; digression metastasizes into the real content.

structures.name: The Anatomy
structures.text: [Menippean — Burton] — stop narrating to dissect one phenomenon exhaustively.

structures.name: The Lipogram / Oulipo Constraint
structures.text: [French] — a hidden rule warps every sentence; the enforced absence mirrors a thematic one.

structures.name: The Rhopalic Snowball
structures.text: [Oulipo/ancient] — each unit one element longer; visible swelling toward rupture.

structures.name: Abecedarian / Acrostic
structures.text: [Hebrew scripture] — an external fixed sequence (the alphabet) governs the beats.

structures.name: Champu
structures.text: [Sanskrit/Kannada] — scheduled alternation of flat prose and heightened verse at the peaks.

structures.name: The Ghazal
structures.text: [Arabic/Persian/Urdu] — self-contained scenes unified by a refrain-image and one mood, never by plot.

structures.name: The Qasīda
structures.text: [pre-Islamic Arabic] — ruined-campsite lament → brutal journey → arrival at the petition/boast.

structures.name: Magic Realism Anchor
structures.text: [Latin American] — the impossible stated in the register of the mundane, never explained.

structures.name: Liturgy of the Hours
structures.text: [monastic] — the eight canonical offices, each its own mood, clock the chapter.

structures.name: The Seder Order
structures.text: [Passover Haggadah] — fixed ritual steps with an embedded "why is tonight different" catechism.

structures.name: The Hexagram
structures.text: [I Ching] — six broken/unbroken beats read as one situation; a "changing line" mutates it into the sequel.

structures.name: The Calendar Round
structures.text: [Mesoamerican] — two clocks of different lengths mesh; catastrophe lands on their alignment.

structures.name: The Ta'ziyeh
structures.text: [Persian passion play] — a communal processional march toward a liturgically foreknown death. Kin: 87.

structures.name: Restoration Arc / Hózhǫ́
structures.text: [Diné — sacred; adapt the logic, not the rite] — disorder → fourfold movement → restored balance, sealed by a repeated closing cadence.

structures.name: Songlines
structures.text: [Aboriginal Australian] — sequence dictated by a geographic route; to tell the story is to walk the land.

structures.name: The Emaki Handscroll
structures.text: [Japanese, iji-dōzu] — one continuous lateral pan, no scene breaks, the figure recurring across moments. Inverse of 54.

structures.name: The Mandala
structures.text: [Hindu/Buddhist] — penetrate nested concentric courts past cardinal guardians toward a central revelation. Inverse of 76.

structures.name: The Memory Palace
structures.text: [classical loci] — walk a remembered architecture; each room stores one beat.

structures.name: The Unicursal Labyrinth
structures.text: [Chartres] — a single inevitable switchbacking path to the center and back; no wrong turns.

structures.name: Perimeter Breach
structures.text: — concentric defenses failing one by one from the outside in. Inverse of 73.

structures.name: Quarantine Lockdown / Shrinking Box
structures.text: — the navigable space contracts scene by scene.

structures.name: Fog of War
structures.text: — information starved to terrifying flashes; jagged, confused pacing. Kin: 79.

structures.name: Sensory Deprivation Box
structures.text: — total isolation; structured purely by memory, hallucination, dread. Kin: 78.

structures.name: Attrition Cascade
structures.text: — tension mapped to a dwindling counter (ammo, oxygen, daylight, sanity).

structures.name: Chain of Command
structures.text: — an order or piece of intel cascades up/down a hierarchy, distorting as it passes.

structures.name: Rasa Engineering
structures.text: [Indian aesthetics] — the chapter built as a delivery machine for one dominant emotion.

structures.name: Stages of Grief
structures.text: — denial/anger/bargaining/depression/acceptance as the literal pacing beats.

structures.name: Cognitive Dissonance
structures.text: — interior monologue continuously contradicts external action and speech.

structures.name: Paranoia Pendulum
structures.text: — rhythmic swings between blinding trust and absolute dread.

structures.name: Intrusive Thought Override
structures.text: — a standard scene repeatedly hijacked by one unignorable thought until it derails.

structures.name: Terminal Clarity
structures.text: — the calm, observant pacing of someone who already knows they've lost. Kin: 69.

structures.name: Monogatari Dialogue Matrix
structures.text: [Japanese] — hyper-fast layered conversation doing the work of a brawl.

structures.name: Flyting
structures.text: [Norse/Scots] — a ritual escalating insult-duel; combat by speech, in rounds. Kin: 90.

structures.name: Katajjaq Duel
structures.text: [Inuit throat-song] — two interlocking voices racing until one breaks. Kin: 89.

structures.name: Commedia Lazzi
structures.text: [Italian] — a loose frame punctuated by recurring stock set-piece "bits."

structures.name: Tarot Spread (Celtic Cross)
structures.text: — ten fixed positions, each meaning framing its scene.

structures.name: Gyan Chaupar
structures.text: [Indian — ancestor of Snakes & Ladders] — moral-board traversal; virtues are sudden ascents, vices sudden plunges.

structures.name: Isekai / Liminal Transition
structures.text: [anime] — the disorienting rules of crossing from a known reality into an alien state.
